name: Abia
known_for: Aba, a hub of small-scale manufacturing
history: Abia was created on 27 August 1991 from Imo State, with Umuahia as the capital. Umuahia served for a time as a seat of the Biafran government during the civil war. Aba, the state's commercial city, grew from a colonial-era trading town into one of Nigeria's busiest centres of cottage industry.
economy: Aba is famous for tailoring, shoemaking, leather goods and a wide range of locally made products sold at Ariaria market and across West Africa. The state also produces crude oil in its southern areas, and Umudike is home to a national root crops research institute and an agricultural university.
fun_facts: Aba-made shoes and garments are sold well beyond Nigeria and are celebrated under the 'Made in Aba' label.
Aba's Enyimba football club won the CAF Champions League in 2003 and 2004.
Aba is the state's commercial centre, while Umuahia is the capital.

name: Adamawa
nickname_variants: Highest Peak of the Nation (newer slogan listed by some sources)
known_for: Sukur Cultural Landscape (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
Yola and the Lamido of Adamawa
history: Adamawa takes its name from the historic Adamawa Emirate, founded by Modibbo Adama as a subordinate kingdom of the Sokoto Caliphate, with Yola founded in 1841 as its capital. Part of the area came under British rule in the early twentieth century, and the eastern portion belonged to the Northern Cameroons until a 1961 referendum joined it to Nigeria. The state was created on 27 August 1991 when Gongola State was split into Adamawa and Taraba.
economy: Agriculture is the main occupation, with livestock and crops such as cotton, groundnuts, millet, cassava, guinea corn and yams. The state government describes its economy as the largest in the North East. The American University of Nigeria in Yola and Adamawa State University in Mubi are major institutions, and the Benue River passes through Yola.
fun_facts: The state covers about 36,900 square kilometres and has 21 local government areas.
It has more than 100 indigenous ethnic groups, one of the most diverse states in Nigeria.
The Sukur Cultural Landscape in the north of the state was among Nigeria's first UNESCO World Heritage listings.

Ibeno Beach on the Atlantic is often described as one of the longest beaches in the region.

known_for: Onitsha Main Market and Niger River port
history: Anambra State was created in 1976 from the East Central State and later lost territory to Enugu in 1991. It is named after the Anambra River. The Igbo-Ukwu archaeological finds, intricate bronzes dated to about the ninth century, make the area one of the oldest centres of metalworking in West Africa.
economy: Anambra is a trading and manufacturing state. Onitsha, on the Niger, has one of the largest markets in West Africa, Nnewi hosts manufacturers of motorcycle and auto parts, and Aba-like clusters of small industry exist across the state. Natural gas deposits have been identified in the Anambra basin.
fun_facts: Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are among the finest early metal artworks found in Africa.
Onitsha sits on the east bank of the River Niger and is a major inland port and market town.

name: Bauchi
known_for: Yankari National Park and Wikki Warm Springs
history: Bauchi was an emirate founded in the early nineteenth century and was brought under British rule as Bauchi Province of the Northern Nigeria Protectorate. It was part of the North-Eastern State until 3 February 1976, when Bauchi State was created; at that time it also included what is now Gombe State, which separated in 1996.
economy: Bauchi is an agricultural state, producing cotton, groundnuts, millet, tomatoes and yams, with irrigation schemes and livestock. Its tourism draws on Yankari, a game reserve opened to visitors in the early 1960s and made a national park in 1991, famous for elephants and the Wikki warm springs. Industries include flour milling and ceramics.
fun_facts: Nigeria's first Prime Minister, Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, is buried in Bauchi.
Yankari lies about 110 km from the state capital.
The state covers about 49,000 square kilometres, roughly 5 percent of Nigeria.

name: Bayelsa
known_for: Home state of former President Goodluck Jonathan
history: Bayelsa was created on 1 October 1996 from Rivers State, and its name combines the first letters of three earlier local government areas. Oloibiri in the state is where commercial crude oil was first discovered in Nigeria in 1956, with production beginning in 1958. Yenagoa is the capital, and the Ijaw are the main ethnic group.
economy: Oil and gas are the dominant sources of state revenue, though the oil fields at Oloibiri are largely depleted. The state is a network of rivers, creeks and swamp forest, so fishing, boat transport and small-scale farming matter locally. It has had one of the smallest populations among Nigerian states.
fun_facts: Nigeria's first commercial oil discovery was made at Oloibiri in 1956.
Bayelsa is largely made up of waterways and low-lying land.
Goodluck Jonathan, who served as president from 2010 to 2015, is from Bayelsa.

name: Benue
known_for: Yams, rice, cassava, maize and soybeans
history: Benue grew out of the Benue Province of the colonial Northern Region and then the Benue-Plateau State, formed in the 1960s. Disputes between the Benue and Plateau blocs led to the split, and Benue State was created for its half on 3 February 1976, with Makurdi as capital. In 1991 the Igala-speaking part of the state was combined with areas of Kwara to form Kogi State.
economy: Agriculture is the backbone of the economy and employs most of the workforce; the state is widely called the Food Basket of the Nation for its yams, cassava, maize, rice and soybeans. The Benue River floodplain provides fertile land, and the state also has a range of mineral deposits. Higher education includes Benue State University and the Federal University of Agriculture, Makurdi.
fun_facts: The state is named after the Benue River, one of Nigeria's largest rivers after the Niger.
The state government says more than 30 distinct ethnic groups live in Benue.
The 2006 census counted about 4.25 million people in the state.

name: Borno
known_for: Sambisa and Chad Basin conservation areas
history: Borno was the core of the Kanem-Bornu Empire, one of the longest-lasting states in African history, which ruled the Lake Chad region for roughly a thousand years until its conquest in the late nineteenth century. Britain took control around 1902. Borno State was created on 3 February 1976 from the North-Eastern State, and Yobe was later separated from it in 1991.
economy: The traditional economy rests on farming, fishing in the Lake Chad basin and livestock, with Maiduguri as the main trading centre. The state borders Niger, Chad and Cameroon, so cross-border trade has long mattered. Lake Chad has shrunk dramatically, which has hurt fishing and farming communities.
fun_facts: Borno shares international borders with Niger, Chad and Cameroon.
Its history as a centre of Islamic learning and empire stretches back over a millennium.
It is one of the largest states in Nigeria by area.

economy: Tourism is a priority, built around the Calabar Carnival, the Obudu plateau and the rainforest. The state also grows cocoa, palm produce and timber, and Calabar's port and export processing zone support trade and light industry.

The rainforests of the state shelter rare primates including the Cross River gorilla.

name: Edo
known_for: Benin Kingdom and the Oba of Benin
history: Edo was created on 27 August 1991 from Bendel State. Benin City was the capital of the powerful Kingdom of Benin, famed for its bronze and ivory art and for the vast earthen walls and moats around the city. British forces sacked the city in 1897 and removed thousands of works, now known worldwide as the Benin Bronzes, many of which are still held in foreign museums.
economy: Edo's economy mixes agriculture (rubber, oil palm, cocoa, cassava and timber), trade, some oil production, and services centred on Benin City. Traditional craft guilds, particularly bronze casting, continue in the city.
fun_facts: The Benin Bronzes are among the most celebrated works of African art and the subject of ongoing return efforts.
The earthen walls of old Benin were among the largest man-made earthworks of their time.
The Oba of Benin remains an influential traditional ruler.

name: Enugu

economy: Coal mining dominated the economy through the mid-twentieth century. Today Enugu's economy is more diversified, with trade, education, public administration and a growing services and technology sector. The University of Nigeria, Nsukka, is in the state.

name: Federal Capital Territory (Abuja)
history: The Federal Capital Territory was created by Decree No. 6 of 1976, announced on 4 February 1976 by the Murtala Muhammed government after a panel chaired by Justice Aguda recommended a central, sparsely populated site to replace congested Lagos. The territory was carved out of parts of Niger, Kwara and Plateau, and the Federal Capital Development Authority planned and built the new city through the 1980s. The seat of government formally moved from Lagos to Abuja on 12 December 1991. The original town called Abuja was renamed Suleja so the name could be used for the new capital.
economy: The economy is driven by government and administration, with federal ministries, agencies, embassies and the National Assembly concentrated in the city. Construction, real estate, banking, hospitality and other services grew around the relocation of federal institutions, and satellite towns supply the capital with labour and farm produce. Lagos remains the country's main commercial centre.
fun_facts: Abuja was built from scratch as a planned capital, chosen partly for its central location and neutrality among major ethnic groups.
Zuma Rock, a huge monolith on the road into the city, is called the 'Gateway to Abuja'.
The territory is administered by a minister appointed by the president rather than by an elected governor.

name: Kaduna
known_for: Former capital of the Northern Region
Nok culture heritage in the south
history: Kaduna was founded by the British around 1913 and served as the capital of the Northern Region until 1967. The state was created in 1967 as North-Central State and renamed Kaduna State in 1976, and Katsina was later split from it in 1987. The ancient city of Zaria, seat of the Zazzau Emirate, lies within the state, and the southern part is linked to the Nok culture, one of West Africa's earliest iron-working societies.
economy: Kaduna has been one of the north's main industrial and educational centres, with a refinery, a once-large textile industry, food processing, and major institutions including Ahmadu Bello University, the Nigerian Defence Academy and aviation training facilities. Agriculture remains important across the state.

name: Kano
history: Kano has one of the longest urban histories in West Africa, rising as a major Hausa city-state and a key hub of trans-Saharan trade, craft production and Islamic scholarship centuries before colonial rule. The British conquered the Kano Emirate in 1903, incorporating it into the Northern Nigeria Protectorate; modern Kano State was formed in 1968.
economy: Kano is the second-largest industrial and commercial centre in Nigeria, with strength in textiles, leather and hides, agricultural produce trading (including one of Africa's largest grain markets, Dawanau Market), and Islamic banking. The centuries-old Kurmi Market remains active today.

known_for: Meeting point of the Niger and Benue rivers

history: Kogi was created on 27 August 1991 from parts of Benue, Niger and Kwara states. Lokoja served as the capital of the Northern Nigeria Protectorate, and Lord Lugard ran the newly amalgamated country from there after 1914.
economy: Agriculture is the mainstay, with cashew, cassava, rice and fishing prominent. The state is rich in solid minerals including coal, limestone, iron ore and tin, which support the Ajaokuta Steel Company, the Itakpe iron ore operation and the Obajana cement factory, one of the largest in Africa.

known_for: Largest state in Nigeria by area
Kainji, Jebba, Shiroro and Zungeru hydropower dams
history: Niger State was created on 3 February 1976 when the former North-Western State was split into Niger and Sokoto states, with Minna as capital. It takes its name from the River Niger, which runs along its western side. The Nupe, Gbagyi, Kamuku, Kambari and Hausa are among the main indigenous peoples, and the state is the home of two former military heads of state, Ibrahim Babangida and Abdulsalami Abubakar.
economy: The state is the acclaimed power house of the nation: Kainji, Jebba and Shiroro dams generate a large share of Nigeria's hydroelectricity, and the newer Zungeru dam adds to it. Fertile land supports most of Nigeria's staple crops and a growing agro-processing sector, and the state has mineral deposits and tourism assets such as Kainji Lake National Park, the largest national park in the country.
fun_facts: Niger covers about 76,000 square kilometres, roughly 8 to 9 percent of Nigeria's land area, making it the largest state.
Kainji Lake National Park is one of Nigeria's largest national parks.
Gurara Falls is one of the best-known waterfalls in the country.

name: Ogun
history: Ogun was created on 3 February 1976 from the old Western State and is named after the Ogun River. Abeokuta, meaning 'under the rock', was founded in the 1830s by Egba people who took refuge around Olumo Rock during the era of regional wars. The state is the birthplace of Wole Soyinka, Fela Kuti and Olusegun Obasanjo.
economy: Ogun is a leading industrial state because of its location beside Lagos, with factories at Agbara, Ota and Sagamu and several large cement plants. Agriculture, including cassava, cocoa and fruit, remains important, and the state has a large number of universities.
fun_facts: Abeokuta's name means 'under the rock', after Olumo Rock.
Wole Soyinka, the first African winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature, was born in Abeokuta.
Ogun is called the Gateway State because it lies on the road and rail routes into Lagos.

name: Ondo
history: Ondo was created on 3 February 1976 from the old Western State and gave up its northern part when Ekiti was created in 1996. Akure is the capital, and the state includes the Ondo and Owo kingdoms and the Ilaje coastal communities in the south.
economy: Ondo is among Nigeria's leading cocoa-producing states, and has large bitumen deposits along its coastal belt that have drawn investor interest. Oil activity occurs in its coastal and offshore areas, and farming, forestry and fishing are important.
fun_facts: Ondo is widely cited as one of Nigeria's top cocoa producers.
The Idanre Hills, with their steps and old settlement ruins, are a major tourist site.
The state is known for large bitumen reserves.

name: Osun
known_for: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
Ile-Ife, regarded as the cradle of the Yoruba
history: Osun was created on 27 August 1991 from Oyo State and is named after the Osun River and its goddess. Ile-Ife in the state is traditionally regarded as the origin of the Yoruba people, and the city produced remarkable bronze and terracotta heads in the medieval period. The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
economy: Osun's economy combines farming (cocoa, kola nut, yam, cassava), small-scale gold mining and trade, along with education and tourism. The annual Osun-Osogbo Festival draws devotees and visitors from around the world.
fun_facts: The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove is one of the few remaining areas of primary forest in southern Nigeria.
Ile-Ife is considered the spiritual home of the Yoruba people.
Obafemi Awolowo University is located in Ile-Ife.

name: Oyo
known_for: University of Ibadan, Nigeria's first university
history: Oyo State was created in 1976 from the old Western State and takes its name from the Old Oyo Empire, a powerful Yoruba kingdom that dominated the region for centuries. Ibadan, founded in the 1820s, grew into one of Africa's largest cities and served as the capital of the Western Region, where the first television station in Africa began broadcasting in 1959.
economy: Ibadan is a major centre of education and trade, hosting the University of Ibadan (founded 1948), the University College Hospital and the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture. Cocoa, food crops and markets support the wider economy, and Ogbomoso and Oyo town are other significant centres.
fun_facts: The University of Ibadan, founded in 1948, was Nigeria's first university.
Cocoa House in Ibadan was an early skyscraper in West Africa.
Western Nigeria Television, launched in Ibadan in 1959, is often cited as Africa's first television station.

name: Plateau
known_for: Jos Plateau scenery and cool climate
history: In May 1967 the Benue and Plateau provinces were merged into Benue-Plateau State, which was split in 1976 to create Plateau State with Jos as its capital. British tin mining began on the plateau in 1902 and turned Jos into a mining and trading centre that drew migrants from across Nigeria. In 1996 the western half of Plateau State was separated to form Nasarawa State.
economy: Tin and columbite mining shaped the economy for most of the twentieth century and left behind many lakes and gorges. Today the state relies on agriculture, trade in Jos, light industry such as food processing and brewing, and tourism built on the plateau's hills, rocks, waterfalls and museums. The University of Jos is one of the country's large universities.
fun_facts: Jos is still often called 'Tin City' after its mining past.
The Jos Plateau is the source of several northern rivers, including the Kaduna and Gongola.
The state is home to more than 50 ethnic groups, often described as a small version of Nigeria.

name: Rivers
history: The area was part of the Oil Rivers Protectorate from 1885, later the Niger Coast Protectorate, before joining the colony of Southern Nigeria. Rivers State was created in 1967 from the former Eastern Region, built around the oil-rich Niger Delta.
economy: Rivers is one of Nigeria's leading oil- and gas-producing states, with major petroleum infrastructure, refining and petrochemical facilities, and busy seaports. Port Harcourt is the commercial centre of the Nigerian oil industry, with significant logistics, banking and service activity.
fun_facts: Port Harcourt is nicknamed the Garden City.
The state was created in 1967 from the old Eastern Region and is built around the oil-rich Niger Delta.
Port Harcourt has been a hub of the oil industry for decades.

name: Sokoto
known_for: Seat of the Sokoto Caliphate and the Sultan of Sokoto
history: Sokoto was founded in the early nineteenth century as the capital of the Sokoto Caliphate, established after the 1804 jihad led by Usman dan Fodio, which united most Hausa states into one of West Africa's largest empires. The British took Sokoto in 1903. The Sultan of Sokoto remains a leading Muslim authority in Nigeria. Sokoto State was created in 1976 from the North-Western State, and Kebbi and Zamfara were later separated from it.
economy: Sokoto has a farming and livestock economy, with millet, sorghum, rice, onions and goat skins prized for leather. The state has limestone deposits used for cement, and trade with neighbouring Niger is important. Usmanu Danfodiyo University is among its major institutions.
fun_facts: The Sultan of Sokoto is regarded as the spiritual head of Nigeria's Muslims.
Former president Shehu Shagari was from Sokoto State.
The Sokoto Caliphate was one of the largest states in nineteenth-century Africa.

name: Taraba
history: Taraba was created on 27 August 1991 when Gongola State was divided into Taraba and Adamawa. The area includes the historic Jukun heartland around Wukari and the highland communities of the Mambilla Plateau. Jalingo is the capital.
economy: Agriculture is central, with maize, rice, sorghum, yams, tea and coffee, and cattle rearing on the cool Mambilla grasslands. The plateau is also the site of long-discussed hydropower plans, and the state has mineral deposits. Tourism assets include the national park and mountain scenery.
fun_facts: Chappal Waddi, on the Taraba side of the Nigeria-Cameroon border, is generally cited as the highest point in Nigeria.
Gashaka-Gumti National Park, shared with Adamawa, is among the largest protected areas in the country.
The Mambilla Plateau has Nigeria's most extensive tea growing area.

name: Yobe
history: Yobe was carved out of Borno State on 27 August 1991, with Damaturu as capital. The state takes its name from the Yobe (Komadugu Yobe) river along its northern border. Its towns, such as Potiskum, Gashua and Nguru, grew as trading centres on routes linking Hausaland and the Kanem-Bornu region.
economy: Yobe lies in the Sahel and relies on farming, livestock and trade. Common products include groundnuts, cowpeas, millet, sorghum and gum arabic, and Potiskum is a busy market for grain, livestock and hides. The Hadejia-Nguru wetlands support fishing, irrigation farming and migratory birds.
fun_facts: The state is named after the Yobe river.
The Hadejia-Nguru wetlands are an internationally important habitat for migratory birds.
Potiskum is one of the main commercial towns in north-eastern Nigeria.
verify: Drafted from general knowledge. Yobe has been affected by the Boko Haram insurgency; check current conditions before featuring it for visitors.

name: Zamfara
known_for: Early adoption of sharia criminal law
history: Zamfara was one of the historic Hausa kingdoms before being absorbed into the Sokoto Caliphate. The present state was created on 1 October 1996 from Sokoto State, with Gusau as capital. In 1999 to 2000 it became the first Nigerian state to extend sharia law to criminal matters, a move other northern states later followed.
economy: Farming is the backbone, with millet, sorghum, groundnuts and cotton, alongside livestock. The state has gold deposits that are largely mined artisanally. Gusau is the main commercial centre.
fun_facts: Zamfara was the first state to adopt sharia criminal law in the post-1999 period.
Gusau is a major grain and livestock trading town.
It is one of the six states created in 1996.
verify: Drafted from general knowledge. Zamfara has been severely affected by banditry and illegal mining violence; check current conditions before featuring it to visitors.
